title: What is Proof-of-Work?
transcript_text: If Bitcoin is fully decentralized, how can transactions be moved between users? Who selects where transactions go and how they get there? Bitcoin uses what is called a proof-of-work consensus mechanism to create agreement on where transactions go across the network. A consensus mechanism is a way to make a group of people form a collective decision. There's many consensus mechanisms in computer science. Proof-of-work was chosen for Bitcoin because it bestudes Bitcoin's radical innovation of linking computers and money. The mechanism requires anyone who wants to move Bitcoin from point A to point B to submit work to the network or pay a fee for someone to do it on their behalf. This work is called mining. Miners must expend energy to solve a puzzle of sorts that allows them to add blocks to the blockchain. After it's complete, the work of solving new blocks can easily be verified by other users. With digital work, Bitcoin effectively creates a form of artificial cost in a usually costless digital world. Anyone wishing to amend or alter the blockchain's transaction record must complete expensive work that's also trivially easy for others to verify. With the cost of proof-of-work comes the benefit of security. Proof-of-work serves as a real cost to create a new Bitcoin and a protection mechanism against bad actors who might try to alter the blockchain's transaction record. Bitcoin users can trust that the network's transaction record is valid because only values that miners have expended energy on can make it into the Bitcoin larger. Any attempt to replace or alter previous transactions requires an equivalent amount of work used to create the transaction plus the work dedicated to all the other transactions stacked below in the blockchain. In other words, an attacker would have to burn enormous amounts of energy to rewrite past transactions.

title: CNBC - Bitfarms CEO says ‘strengthening U.S. exposure’ big part of Stronghold Digital acquisition
transcript_text: Last week, we learned that after three years of merger discussions, Bitfarm's entered into an agreement to acquire competitor stronghold digital mining. Bitfarm says the merger will cost around $125 million in stock, and around another $50 million of debt. The deal is expected to close in key one of next year after approval from regulators. What was behind the decision to join forces with stronghold digital? I'm sure strengthening your US footprint played into the move, but the Bitcoin having back in April have anything to do with it. Yes, so there's a lot of things that came into play here. Definitely strengthening our US exposures. A big part, and we're a very international Bitcoin miner. We've got over 12 sites in four different countries and three languages. But really, US has been the smallest part of our portfolio. So with this one transaction, we're able to increase the size of our portfolio next year by almost 50%. We're able to rebalance our energy portfolio towards the United States. So next year, we're going to have about 65% in North America, and almost half of that in the US. And we're able to get a huge growth pipeline, both in the short term, as well as organic growth growth opportunities over the next couple of years to continue expanding in the United States. So one transaction really ticked a lot of boxes and opportunities for us. It sounds like it. And did the Bitcoin having back in April play a role? So this is something we've been working on for the last three years. The Bitcoin having certainly has compressed margins for everyone. But for a company like Bitfarm's, it would be successful. We have to be thinking so many years in advance. So the reality is, is that for this last having, we were getting ready for it back in 2020. And if anything, this transaction is more geared around getting ready for the next having in 2028. Because that's how forward thinking you have to be in order to survive in this space. Now, of course, this deal comes as M&A activity in the Bitcoin mining space remains red hot. There have been other deals recently, including between Core Scientific and AI Infrastructure startup CoreWeave. As we've seen, the growing trends of Bitcoin miners turning to artificial intelligence to diversify revenue streams. Given it became a lot less profitable to mine Bitcoin post-having, what do you think about this trend? I understand Bitfarm's plans to move into the AI space as well. Was your acquisition of Stronghold pursued with the intent of integrating high-performance computing and AI? Yes, so the high-performance computing trend and the AI trend is very powerful driver right now. What we're looking at is, how do we increase the value of our energy portfolio? And how do we maximize utility of all of our assets? And certainly, we think HPC and AI is a great way for us to continue to expand our presence in the data center space and continue to get the best leverage out of everything that we have. So when we're looking at growth opportunities in the United States, we're looking at what are the opportunities that are not only good for Bitcoin mining, but are also good for HPC and AI. And with the Stronghold transaction, what we've done a lot is the potential for something really groundbreaking. The ability to create a merged HPC AI and Bitcoin mining data center, which will enable us to save a lot of money in terms of the CapEx build out for the HPC AI data center and also drive a lot better economics at the site, and actually drive a more environmentally friendly HPC data center by removing the diesel generating components that usually are in a HPC data center for redundancy. What other steps are you taking to maximize revenue and profit following the having? What can people expect? Perhaps more acquisitions? So we've been upgrading all of our miners this year. We announced a big transformer of fleet upgrade at the end of last year. So we've ordered just five, 88,000 miners that are going to be deployed this year. About half of those have already been deployed in existing facilities. The other half has been deployed throughout the remainder of this year. As we look towards next year, what we're going to be doing is continuing to build on the success that we've had this year, securing more miners to fill out the build out at Stronghold, as well as our recent Sharon Pennsylvania site, and trying to figure out how we incorporate HPC and AI into our portfolio of energy assets for an end of 2025 or a beginning of 2026 timeline. We think that timeline really aligns well with what we anticipate to be the top of the Bitcoin bull market cycle. And that's the time when we want to have the versification into an alternative revenue stream like HPC and AI. Now, of course, BitFarms has been pushing back on attempts to make it the target of an acquisition as well, rejecting a $950 million takeover offer from Riot, which was unsolicited. As of two weeks ago, Riot claims to own a nearly 19% stake of BitFarms. Where does everything stand with Riot right now? What's the latest there? And would you ever be open to a full takeover offer from the firm? We, as a company, are always open to any opportunity that's going to maximize value for shareholders. And so when Riot first came to us a couple of months ago, we started the Strategic Alternate Review Process. We set up a special committee after board, and we looked at all sorts of different opportunities. We ended that Strategic Alternate Review Process a few weeks ago when we basically came to a handshake agreement here with Stronghold in order to facilitate this agreement. Because at that point, the compelling economics of this transaction and the pro-form emerged company are so compelling that that's what we decided to move forward with. And the board unanimously decided that that was the best way to maximize value for all shareholders. We believe that this deal is really transformative for the company and for all of our shareholders, not only for what this enables for our immediate growth and the combined aspects of this company, but what this unlocks for our growth potential next year in the years to come. This is a pivotal transaction where we've really committed to diversifying beyond Bitcoin mining itself, not in a way that's going to distract from Bitcoin mining, but in a way that's going to make us better Bitcoin miners. And so, in addition to expanding our US portfolio with this one transaction, we've also been able to diversify into energy generation, get huge access to energy trading in the United States, largest electricity market, PGM, been able to integrate heat recycling, waste mitigation, as well as HPC and AI into our portfolio. So this has been a very transformative transaction, which is going to be great for all shareholders. Now last month, you were appointed the new CEO of BitFarms after previously serving as chief mining officer. What are your plans for BitFarms in this new role? What's your vision as you're now leading the company? So, the vision here is really to diversify the company beyond Bitcoin mining. Just like I just outlined here, we see a tremendous opportunity in the next 12-15 months to get the most out of the coming Bitcoin bull run. But we need to be thinking far in advance of the coming few months. We need to be thinking one, two, three years ahead. And so, internally, I've outlined plans. I will take us all the way through the 20-28 having event. And that's what we're focused on now. It's not just what's going to be best for BitFarms in the immediate future. But how do we get position for the bull run, the bear market, the subsequent having event in 20-28? And we really think that diversification is a great aspect towards achieving those goals. For us, really, we want to be in control of our energy. Because as a company, as a Bitcoin mining company, energy is our primary driver of costs. And for not a control of our energy, we're not a control of our costs. If we're not a control of our costs, we're not a control of our future. And so, for the company, we really need to be putting greater levels of control in place so that we are in control of that most primary driver for us, which is our energy. So huge growth in our energy portfolio and the diversification elements that will help us survive and thrive in any economic conditions. How expanding on that, you touched on this today. You also mentioned it in a statement last month where you noted that BitFarms is in fact starting to plan and implement strategies for the next having event in 20-28. What are some of those strategies that are being discussed? What can people expect from BitFarms within the next four years ahead of the next having specifically? Thank you and expect us to really grow our footprint in the United States with a very strategic focus on cost controls. We're not a company that's willing to grow for any cost. We've shown this for the last seven years of our operations. We're strategic in everything that we do, whether it be our miner purchases, the countries that we operate in, the new energy contracts that we sign up for. We're very, very strategic and deliberate in that process. I think that the market can expect that we are going to be focused on trying to maximize the opportunity that comes into historic cycles because as a company that's been around for seven years, this is personally, it was my third having and we're now working towards my fourth having event. We understand how these cycles play out every four years and in order to deliver the most value for shareholders, we need to be playing the cycles to the best of their ability. Right now, that's a focus on growing our Bitcoin hash rate as fast as possible and improving efficiencies for that Bitcoin bull run. For 2025 and 2026, this is going to be a focus on diversification and driving down our energy costs. In 2027, we're primarily going to be focusing on rebuilding and expanding our energy infrastructure and in 2028 and the end of 2027, we're going to be focusing probably on doing another fleet upgrade, just like we announced at the end of 2023 and we're conducting right now in 2024.

title: The Future of Bitcoin Mining
transcript_text: So joining me now to talk the state of crypto is Jeff Morphe, CEO of BitFarms. Jeff, welcome. Hi, Kristen. Thanks for having me. All right. So you've got a unique position obviously very in tune to the crypto market at what is driving this momentum of late and can it continue? Well, it can continue. But what's really driving it right now is the excitement from the American ETFs coming on just the demand that they're bringing to the market is unlike anything that's been in existence in the history of Bitcoin since 2009. It's that demand that's feeling it. And with diminished supply coming along with the having, it really sets up for a what should be a wonderful year and wonderful number of years. Walk us through what the having entails and how your company takes part in that. Oh, sure. The having takes place based on the protocols that were designed by Satoshi back in 2009. So to force the industry to continue to adapt, to innovate and to become more efficient every four years, the block rewards are the subsidies that the the whole software provides to us gets chopped in half. So originally there was 50 Bitcoin that were awarded for every block that was solved. And that was back in 2009 and then it's successively every approximately four years chopped in half. So it went from 50 to 25 to 12 and a half to six and a quarter, six and a quarter where we are now for the last four years. And in mid April, it's going to move to three and an eighth. And so it forces all the miners basically to have the same inputs that we had before in terms of electricity or overheads and things like that. But now our revenues, which is basically earned in Bitcoin, will be chopped in half. So it just forces us to be that much more efficient and do a number of other things. And the second part of your question, you asked, what are we doing about it? Well, in November, we made a major announcement for a transformational fleet upgrade where we're buying a whole bunch of approximately 64,000 in total made up of initial order 35, 36,000 miners plus an option for 28,000 more at a very good price. These new series of miners are ultra efficient. So we're going to be able to replace our old miners with much more efficient new miners that uses a lot less electricity and pushes out more. So the efficiency is there. Plus we continue to endeavor to find new locations with lower cost electricity. And that's so critical to the longevity of our company and the industry as well. How do you maintain it or at least try to maintain a level of evenness and steadiness in what is generally a volatile industry if that is a goal of yours, Jeff? It is a volatile industry. We deal in a commodity where there's incredible ups and incredible downs and you need some pretty thick skin on some days to do that. But just like any other commodity industry, it's important to keep your costs and your overheads down. So even when prices go down, you're managing positive cash flow. And when things get really exciting and things go up and margins are up and margins are up, then you're absolutely bringing the best possible returns to shareholders by enhanced cash flow. So it's running a lean and mean operation. And I think that's what we do. And frankly, we've been around for six years. And we've learned from the last having, being one of the sole survivors of that having when things were a lot different. They didn't have the ETFs supercharging the market. But we need to be very, very efficient. And that's what we've really driven our last four years towards. What does this mean for Bitcoin owners, people who own the cryptocurrency outright or invest in it? Well, the whole ecosystem just continues to adapt and evolve. So with the advent of the ETFs, it's giving people public-traded vehicles for going in and out of Bitcoin very easily. That's really opened itself up for institutional adoption. But it's also made it easier for a number of other investors to get a piece of Bitcoin and share in the future of Bitcoin. You can also buy Bitcoin yourself. Some people find that additional complexity to be too much for them. But other people feel very comfortable when they can put their own Bitcoin and their own wallet and know exactly where they are. For the Bitcoin miners, we are part of that ecosystem. We are the utility that makes it work. But it also offers asymmetrical upside and asymmetrical downside to it. As you look at our stock performance, generally when Bitcoin goes up or down, we go up or down three times more. We've got a three beta associated with our stock performance. So if people want to get in and think that the coin is going up, then having exposure to the Bitcoin miners will help get outsized upside if they really believe in Bitcoin. I realistically, when it comes to mining, how much can be done to lessen the load on the environment? Well, quite a bit. In the past, a lot of the miners went for coal sourced electricity and things like that. With the growth of the industry now and the importance of renewables, most of the miners are very much plunging forward with demand response programs, with starting to take some exposure to wind, to various things. For us, we started in problem school back using exclusively hydro. We moved to Washington as well, which is largely hydro. We are also located in Paraguay, which is exclusively hydro, and that's one of the areas where we're really growing. And then we're in Argentina that uses natural gas. But predominantly, we use a renewal hydroelectricity, which is great, because it comes 24 hours a day. So we're able to keep our machines running with incredible uptime. And part of that is because of the use of renewables, and renewables are important. I think you're going to see probably more adoption of nuclear going forward and less to natural gas and certainly less to coal. Interesting. And it comes to mining. What is your position in the U.S. versus other miners around the world? title: The Black Market That Launched Bitcoin
transcript_text: After the 2008 financial crisis, a mysterious figure named Satoshi Nakamoto created Bitcoin, a decentralized, unsensurable currency meant to give people financial sovereignty. Fast forward to today, it's seen as a financial asset owned by billionaires, Wall Street, and governments. But Bitcoin's first proving ground wasn't in boardrooms or balance sheets, but in the shadows of the internet, a place called the Silk Road. If you've heard of it, you likely know it as the first popularized dark web marketplace, which, for better or worse, became Bitcoin's first real use case. When it launched in February 2011, the Silk Road wasn't built to be a digital underworld, it's founder Ross Albrecht, a young libertarian with a background in physics, imagined a free market beyond government control, a place where people could trade directly peer-to-peer without censorship or oversight. However, a marketplace that couldn't be censored also required a currency that couldn't be controlled. Bitcoin still barely two years old at the time fit perfectly. Its transactions were irreversible, borderless, and pseudonymous, with every wallet identified only by a string of letters and numbers. To the users flocking to the Silk Road, that felt like true economic freedom. Within months, the marketplace exploded in scale from a few hundred listings to tens of thousands. Anything from books to drugs could be reviewed like an Amazon listing, bought with Bitcoin and shipped worldwide. But that freedom also drew in riskier listings, firearms, and even alleged hitmen services, even if the marketplace technically prohibited it. And as activity on the Silk Road surged, so did Bitcoin's price. For the first time, Bitcoin was powering a real economy, though one that left the world in more shock than awe. But Bitcoin's pseudonymity wasn't invisibility. Every transaction still lived forever on the blockchain, a public ledger that anyone could read. That transparency became the very thread that investigators would later pull. By 2013, a joint team of the FBI and Homeland Security was tracing the movement of coins across addresses. Ross Albrecht, operating under the alias Dred Pirate Roberts, made a series of small but crucial mistakes, reusing handles, logging into forums, leaving behind digital breadcrumbs that led back to him. When FBI agents finally arrested Ross and seized his laptop in a San Francisco library, they captured control of the Silk Road servers and with it, more than 144,000 Bitcoin, still the largest BTC seizure to date. The fall of the Silk Road made global headlines. For many outsiders, Bitcoin became synonymous with dark web crime and money laundering. Its reputation was scorched. But despite the controversy, the network itself never stopped running. No government could switch it off. In practice, Bitcoin had just proven what it was built for, censorship resistance. Over the next years, the narrative began to shift. The US government auctioned off seized coins. What was once criminal evidence became an investment. Today, the currency that once powered a black market economy sits on corporate balance sheets, in regulated funds, and even in national treasuries. The code barely changed, but the context around it surely has. And if you're wondering just how private is Bitcoin really, then watch this next.

title: Best Bitcoin Desktop Wallet?? Electrum Tutorial 2026
transcript_text: If you're serious about holding your own Bitcoin, Electrum is a wallet worth paying attention to. Now, it's been around since 2011. It's open source, Bitcoin only, and trusted by many power users. Unlike beginner wallets that abstract away the details, Electrum shows you exactly what's happening and lets you control it directly. Now, it has a mobile version, but we'll be focusing on the desktop wallet in this video. Let's start by downloading Electrum from the official site, Electrum.org. Now, guys, always double check that you're on the real site. We don't want to download malware from Fishing Clones. Okay, once installed, launch Electrum and you land in the wallet creation wizard. Name your wallet, hit next, and choose what kind you want. For most people, standard wallet is the way to go. You get a 12-word recovery phrase and full control. If you want extra protection, Electrum also supports to factor authentication. It works by requiring a time-based code from Google Authenticator before any transaction can be sent. So even if someone does get your wallet file, they still can't spend your Bitcoin without that code. The multi-seq option lets you go fully custom. Set up wallets that require multiple signatures, like two of three or three of five. This is great for shared custody or spreading risk across devices. Lastly, you can import private keys or addresses, and that's useful for restoring older wallets using private keys or creating a watch-only wallet using Bitcoin addresses, which means you simply monitor wallet activity without putting your private keys on that device. So we'll go with standard. So choose create new seed, back up those 12 words, confirm, set a password, and Electrum boots up your new wallet. Once it opens, you'll see Electrum's main interface, a menu bar up top, tabs like history, send, and receive in the middle, and a status bar at the bottom. We'll be coming back to many of these as we dig into Electrum's more advanced features. But let's start with one that you'll probably use a lot, fee control. Most wallets handle fees in the background, but Electrum lets you have full control. So you can decide how fast you want your transactions confirmed. To test this out, head to the send tab, fill in a recipient address and amount. If you also want to see the Fiat value go to tools, then click on preferences from the drop down, navigate to the Fiat tab, and choose your local currency, and you can also change Bitcoin units here. So back in the send tab. Click pay, and you'll get the fee slider. From the fee policy drop down, Electrum gives you three estimation modes that you can pick between. The first one, ETA mode, targets confirmation within a specific number of blocks. Menpool mode bases the fee on how many transactions are waiting, placing yours at a certain depth in the queue. Fee rate mode is fully manual. You pick the exact sets per byte, but set it to low, and it might never confirm. Now these modes exist to help you interpret the fee market better, and pick the tradeoff between speed versus cost that fits what you're trying to do, rather than hoping that the wallet picks something reasonable. Another one of Electrum's most powerful features is manual coin control, especially if you care about privacy. When you receive Bitcoin, each payment becomes a separate spendable chunk called a UTXO. Most wallets just auto select some combination of these to cover your next transaction, but this might accidentally link parts of your financial activity that should stay separate, like your business and personal wallets. So Electrum lets you override all of that by giving you complete control over which coins get spent. So to access this, go to the top menu, click view, then select show coins, and you'll now see a new coins tab appear next to your usual ones like history and addresses inside the coins tab. You'll see a detailed list of all your UTXOs. So each line shows the amount, the source transaction, and the address that it belongs to. So from here, you can manually select exactly which coins that you want to spend. Once you select it, right click it, and choose add to coin control. Then you'll see a message at the bottom of Electrum's window, and it says coin control active. So this means that your next transaction will use only the UTXOs that you just selected. Everything else will be ignored temporarily. Another tool in your coin control arsenal is freezing, and either the coins or addresses tab, you can right click on any entry, whether it's an individual coin or an entire address, and choose freeze. So this tells Electrum to not touch these funds no matter what. And this is useful for cold funds that you don't want to accidentally spend, or for UTXOs tied to activity that you'd rather not mingle with other transactions. Electrum also gives you full control over the servers that it connects to, something that most wallets handle silently in the background. By default, Electrum connects to public servers to fetch your transaction history, balance, and to broadcast transactions. And these servers don't have access to your private keys, so they can't steal your coins, but they can still log your data and build a profile of your activity. So to avoid this, Electrum lets you manually select which server to connect to, or even better run your own Electrum server for maximum trust and privacy. If you're not running your own, you can still protect your privacy by using Tor. So Tor hides your IP address by routing your traffic through a global network of servers. And this makes it much harder for Electrum servers to link your activity to your identity. To set this up, first download the Tor browser from TorProject.org, connect to the Tor network. Once Tor browser is up and connected, head into Electrum. Then click on the network icon in the bottom right corner or go to Tools and the Network. In the window that opens, select the Proxy tab. Now check the Use Proxy box. In the drop-down select, socks5-tor, and in the host field type 127.0.0.0.1, then set the port to 9050. This tells Electrum to send all its traffic through the Tor network that's already running on your machine. Basically, it hides your connection, so the servers that you talk to don't see your real IP address. Once this is done, close the network window, and you'll know that it's working when Electrum's circular icon in the bottom right turns blue, and that means that it successfully connected through Tor. Electrum also supports the Lightning network, which is Bitcoin's second layer for fast and cheap payments, and it works by letting you open a payment channel with another user. Send Bitcoin instantly with very low fees, and only settle the final result on chain when the channel closes. So you can open channels using the channels tab if it's not visible, enable it via the View menu. Then pick a node to connect to, decide how much to commit from your on-chain wallet and Electrum will handle the setup. Once a channel is open, sending a Lightning payment is easy. Just paste a Lightning invoice into the send tab. Electrum recognizes it automatically and switches into Lightning Mode to receive. Go to the receive tab, switch to Lightning, and generate an invoice like you would for an on-chain request. Channel management happens in the channels tab. You can view your balances, status, and close them when needed. And with that, you're ready to start using some of Electrum's most powerful features. Now, yes, it asks a bit more of you than your average wallet, but in return, you get control and transparency and that is hard to beat. As with all things, Bitcoin, take your time. Start small, try a test transaction or two, and build confidence as you go. And also, let us know how your Electrum journey goes in the comments below. Bye.

transcript_text: Dom Chu is out of the conference and Hester Pierce is with him now she's Commissioner at the SEC. Welcome. Thank you so much Kelly and thank you SEC Commissioner Hester Purse for taking the time to join with us right now in the exchange. Kelly mentioned it the SEC in this iteration is very focused on some of the emerging products that are out there not just in the markets overall but that how they're being wrapped so to speak into exchange traded products. I wonder if you might be able to tell us a little bit about why you're here at the conference and just how you feel about some of these newer type products being made accessible more so to the investing public. Well I'm here because this is such an important segment of what we regulate and so I'm interested in hearing from people about what they're seeing and what the new trends are and and also I just want to comment as a regulator to say we want to work with people on new products and we think it's a it's it's a wrapper that can be useful and and we want to do it in a way that respects investor protection and also the statute but we're willing to work with people. One of the things that has been brought to light more recently within the SEC's purview is the use of levered funds and we know that the SEC itself has made some decisions very recently with regard to maybe throttling back some of the developments around funds that use even more leverage than say existing products that have triple leverage associated with them. Can you take us a little bit through the thought process within the regulatory framework about just why some of these more levered products are being treated with more scrutiny these days especially when it comes to using more leverage. As an initial matter we we are not a merit regulator and so I think that's really important to establish the existing rules do have some limits on leverage in in them and so people can come in with products that are higher than 200 percent but they need to be able to explain how it how it's consistent with the statute and you know again it's not our job to say which products are good or bad it is our job to work with sponsors to make sure that they're disclosing what those products are what the risks are what they're intended to be used for. Now also with regard to cryptocurrencies and tokenization more broadly we know that the SEC is working a lot more with the idea of a broadening out of products tied to tokenization of financial instruments. Would you be able to shed some light on how you view tokenization these of the some of these exchange trade of products and what can be wrapped in them as well as the SEC has made a decision recently with regard to the wisdom tree digital treasury money market fund and being able to provide intraday liquidity for a mutual fund product those all seem like they're at the forefront on a more expansive campaign to tokenize financial products is that correct. Well again it's not the SEC's job to decide what the market how the market moves forward but tokenization is one of those areas that since the administration changed and since the attitude toward crypto and blockchain changed people have come to us and they said we really think tokenization has potential here. Now of course tokenization of money market funds is something that had been worked on for a long time but but you know as you say there's some new developments there and more generally I think people are looking at where it would be most useful putting things on chain could be quite useful in many in many aspects.
